page8_img_1.png.title: Survey: CFar analysis comments' effect on productivity and code quality
page8_img_1.png.description: A two-bar stacked chart reporting field-deployment survey responses about CFar analysis comments. Each bar shows percentages of respondents who said the comments decreased (red), had no effect/neutral (gray), or increased (green) the metric. For productivity (left bar) about 38% said CFar increased their productivity, 19% said it decreased productivity, and the remainder were neutral. For code quality (right bar) about 48% reported increased quality, only ~3% reported decreased quality, and the rest were neutral, indicating overall more respondents saw benefits than harms.

page4_img_1.png.title: CFar progress pane showing build status, analysis warnings, and reviewer state
page4_img_1.png.description: Screenshot of the CFar progress interface reporting iteration-1 build and analysis status. The top box shows a requested build with a CloudBuild/OACR URL; the next box reports “Build succeeded for iteration 1. Processing comments...”. A following message states “Found 1 analysis warnings and 4 warnings from the baseline in iteration 1.” At the bottom is a green status indicator next to a dropdown labeled “ByDesign,” representing CFar’s comment/decision state in the CodeFlow UI. The panel illustrates how CFar surfaces build progress and the number of automated analysis warnings back into the review.

page3_img_1.png.title: CFar-extended CodeFlow interface with automated reviewer callouts
page3_img_1.png.description: A labeled overview of the CFar-extended CodeFlow review UI showing how the automated reviewer (OACR) integrates into normal review workflows. The central panel (a) is the code-diff view with added (green) and removed (red) lines; thin connector lines map analysis warnings to exact code locations. Callout (b) shows a CFar-generated comment box with a yellow header, explanatory text and the three feedback buttons (useful / not useful / do not understand) plus per-button counts; (c) shows a typical human comment (blue), and (f) shows the comment-summary listing where both kinds appear. The figure also highlights the changeset file explorer (g), a highlighted code snippet in the diff (e), and the reviewer-status area (d) where the automated reviewer (“OACR”) is listed and can affect approval when its comments are resolved.

page4_img_2.png.title: CFar-extended CodeFlow architecture
page4_img_2.png.description: A labeled architecture diagram showing how CFar integrates with existing tools: blue boxes are existing components (CodeFlow UI, CodeFlow Web Service, Azure, CloudBuild, and OACR) and green boxes are CFar components (CFar Extension and CFar Web Service). The CFar Extension augments the CodeFlow UI, while the CFar Web Service mediates between the CodeFlow Web Service and the build/analysis backend: it invokes CloudBuild, uploads/clones repositories to Azure, and receives analysis results from OACR. Arrows indicate bidirectional communication between CodeFlow and CFar, between CFar and CloudBuild, between CloudBuild and Azure, and between CloudBuild and the OACR analysis framework; the CFar Web Service posts analysis warnings back into CodeFlow as review comments.

page8_img_3.png.title: Survey: Usefulness and liking of CFar analysis comments
page8_img_3.png.description: A pair of stacked vertical bars shows respondents’ attitudes (percentage on the y‑axis) to two survey questions about CFar analysis comments. The left bar ("I found the analysis comments unuseful or useful?") is overwhelmingly green: a large central segment (~75%) labeled “Useful,” a smaller top green segment (~15–18%) labeled “Very useful,” and a thin red bottom segment (~5–8%) labeled “Unuseful.” The right bar ("I dislike or like having analysis warnings displayed as review comments?") likewise shows most respondents in green (combined “Like” and “Strongly like” around ~75%), a gray neutral band of about ~15–25%, and a very small red “Dislike” slice (~0–5%). These results align with the paper’s reporting that nearly all field respondents found CFar’s comments useful and a strong majority liked having analysis warnings shown in the review interface.

page6_img_1.png.title: Stacked survey bars showing CFar's effect on collaboration and conversations
page6_img_1.png.description: Two vertically stacked-bar charts (Figure 4) summarize field-deployment survey responses about CFar’s impact on communication. The left bar asks whether ‘‘the analysis comments enhanced collaboration among developers’’ and shows a large green portion (about 61% total for ‘‘Agree’’ + ‘‘Strongly agree’’), a smaller gray neutral segment, and a thin red band of disagreement, on a y‑axis labeled ‘‘Percentage of respondents’’ (0–100%). The right bar asks whether ‘‘the analysis comments inspired fewer or more conversations’’ and shows roughly 45% in green (‘‘More’’ + ‘‘Significantly more’’), a larger neutral (gray) middle portion, and a small red ‘‘Fewer’’ segment. The figure therefore indicates that a clear majority perceived improved collaboration and that nearly half reported the comments led to more review conversations, while a nontrivial fraction remained neutral or reported reduced communication.

page7_img_1.png.title: CFar‑inspired conversation topics in code reviews
page7_img_1.png.description: Horizontal bar chart from the field-deployment survey showing the percentage of respondents who reported which topics CFar prompted them to discuss during code reviews. Coding style and Implementation details were the most frequently cited topics (each about 48–49% of respondents), followed by Refactoring (~39%), Other (~25%), Code smells (~18%), and High‑level design (~17–18%). The “Other” category included items such as unit tests, performance, educating junior programmers, and build-breaking issues (none received more than two responses). The distribution shows that CFar sparked both shallow-topic conversations (e.g., style and implementation details) and deeper design/refactoring discussions.

page8_img_2.png.title: Top-10 analysis warnings CFar posted (by proportion)
page8_img_2.png.description: A vertical bar chart showing the top ten types of analysis warnings CFar posted during the field deployment, with the y-axis as proportion of posted warnings (percent). The most frequent warning category is “Validate parameter” at roughly one-third of warnings (≈34%), followed by “Use generic version” (≈16%) and “Replace generic type” (≈15%). The remaining categories — e.g., “Use XmlReader or XmlWriter”, “Call Dispose”, “Set XmlResolver”, “Use load that takes XmlReader”, “Unused instance”, and “Use StringBuilder” — each account for much smaller shares (generally between about 6% and 2–4%). These proportions (from the field-deployment logs of CFar’s 149 analysis comments) reflect that the automated reviewer mainly surfaced shallow, API-usage and style/robustness issues such as parameter validation, generic usage, XML API patterns, disposal, unused instances, and string-construction inefficiencies.
